title: A Black lawyer holds the instruments; the band scatters
summary: Whyte left with a few players while Smith, Lester Young, Abe Bolar and others stayed; a lawyer named Butts held the instruments for payment.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: So then what happened? Zack Whyte went back to Cincinnati.
Yeah, he went on back to Cincinnati and...
He didn't take any of the guys with him?

He took White, Leroy White, and I think two or three of the boys rode with him, and then the others stayed there and sent telegrams home to some of their relatives to send them money, and they sent them money and they went on back to Missouri. But Lester Young and Abe Bolar and all a bunch of us... There was eight of us. Ernie Williams and all of us. They

wanted to stay with me.

So I ran up on a boy, didn't even know his (?), that knew me from Texas. He lived way out on the edge of town there. He used to play music, and he quit playing, and he was working in some factory there. He'd heard about it, and he come down and said, "Buster, come on out to the house. I ain't got no money, but anyway I got two dollars and eighty cents, and you can have that." He said, "Come out to the house, and I'll buy you all some lunch meat. I know you all want to get out of town." He heard about we gonna hobo, and he said, "I'll give you something to eat on." So he give us that two dollars and eighty cents, and gave us some lunch meat that he could hustle. We put it in the sack, in the boxes, and I put it all about my waist here, and I had a big box hanging there, and one sack of tobacco...
Did you have your instruments with you?

No! The sheriff had the instruments. But then what happened, a colored lawyer, his name is Butts, he sent for us to come up to his office. So we went up to his office there. He had the instruments up there. He said, "I got your instruments." Said, "you all can't git 'em, so all you can do is stay here and play." We said, "We can't make no money out there at that place. The man put us out of the hotel. Now we got to get away from here." He said, "Well, I'll tell you what to do. Now, I'm going to keep the instruments here. See, I done paid

the sheriffs; they charged you'all two hundred dollars. I got the instruments here. They're back there in my room. Go back and look." And we went down and looked at it. Everything was sitting back there. He said, "Now, you'all go somewhere and get the money and send it back herè, and send the money back, each man send the money, what you owe in some way... And I own what you own. I own a bass fiddle." He said, "Whoever sends his money for an instrument, I'll put it on the train and send it to you."
Did you get the instruments back?

Yeah, we got them back. He sent them all back. But I think two or three of the boys didn't get theirs. They bought some new ones. And I think a couple of the trumpet players stole their trumpets out of the case. The sheriff went with the case, he thought he was holding it in there, but the boy took his horn out the window. And the sheriff went with the (?) case. He didn't know! Heh-heh! I think Leroy White was one of them that got away with his trumpet.
Oh, I see. You mean, when he sent the instrument in to be attached, he hadn't put the trumpet in it. He kept the trumpet.
No, no. See, when we get through playing that night...
You just had the case in it.
He just turned it back there. And the sheriff and

them were sitting back there and looking, and they said, "All right," and we just sent the instruments right down there where they'd pick them up, and they'd come out there and put them in a squad car and come on back uptown, where they were (?) with the case -- and they wasn't in there. But the drummer couldn't do that. But all the saxophones...we just let them stay there.
We all got 'em back. We hoboed...
